title: Mistakes, LinkedIn and the messages we are creating
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton reflects on an unusually strong response to his LinkedIn complaint that school posts are bland, self-congratulatory and free of mistakes. Working through several reader comments, he argues that such posts say little that differentiates a school, are aimed at no clear audience, and leave out the very thing schools exist for, which is helping students get better. He ties this to his Hedgehog Concept idea: if learning truly drives a school's decisions it should show up in everything it communicates, including the messy phases of struggle. He also challenges the supposed tension between great learning and great income, since families are drawn by evidence that children are improving. He ends with a call for schools to be transparent about how they are improving learning.
points: Bland, similar school social media posts fail on marketing grounds because they convey no point of difference and have no clear audience.
When learning is a school's guiding concept it should be visible in all communication, including honest accounts of mistakes and struggle.
Confidence to share failure is something a school builds by treating a failed lesson as professional work rather than as evidence against the teacher.
Great learning and great income are not opposed, because showing evidence of improvement is what builds parent confidence and enrolment.
quotes: When they don’t, they misrepresent to themselves, their children, students and other stakeholders what learning is and how it happens. Most mistakes are not something to hide. For our children and students we need them to be out in the open.

First, the messages are too smooth, too superficial and too similar. If I wear my marketing hat for a moment, messages should be conveying a point of difference, something that makes us stand out from others. Most of the LinkedIn messages from schools are all pointlessly bland and pointlessly similar.

To put it in a nutshell: What do schools think the gain is from these self-congratulatory and similarly bland LinkedIn posts here and for whom? What is it that is worth the time and energy used to create them?

Gaining the confidence of a community, individually and organisationally, happens when we can show that we are able to support all of our students through each of the rather messy phases that are a part of the learning process. Confidence doesn’t grow when we ignore the very thing that children, students and their parents want most.

I’m not saying here that there aren’t other factors involved in increasing student enrolment. But the missed opportunity is this: Rather than separate great learning and great income, it would help schools to see that great learning is one of the most important drivers of higher enrolment and greater income.

Learning is messy and complex. We need spaces where schools and teachers can discuss and share that complexity and learn from each other. LinkedIn was supposed to be this space but it has been hijacked.
